title: Money and happiness
hook: researchers who disagreed ran a joint study and found happiness mostly keeps rising with income, except for the least happy

segments.voice: Yesterday: we adapt, the lottery winners who were no happier than their neighbors. Your line was we adapt. What ordinary thing did you give a second look? Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

Does money buy happiness? Two serious researchers gave two different answers. Daniel Kahneman, with the economist Angus Deaton, had found that day-to-day happiness seemed to level off above a certain income. Another researcher, Matthew Killingsworth, using a different method, found it kept rising. They could have kept answering each other in print. They chose something else. They sat down together, with a third researcher as referee, and went looking for the truth in the same data.
screen: `TWO RESEARCHERS, TWO ANSWERS.` → `A THIRD AS REFEREE.` → `THE SAME DATA, TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: First, the method. Killingsworth, Kahneman and the psychologist Barbara Mellers published their joint work in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences. It's called an adversarial collaboration: people who disagree design the test together, so nobody can stack the deck. Second, the finding. For most people, day-to-day happiness kept rising as income rose, with no clear ceiling. But the rise works in proportion: the same raise means more to someone with less. Third, the exception, and it's what reconciled the two camps. For the least happy group, happiness rose with income only up to a point, then flattened. The authors suggest that for those people, the deepest sources of misery, like grief, heartbreak or depression, aren't things a bigger paycheck can fix. Money helps a lot of things. It doesn't reach everything. Fourth, an old warning that fits the exception. In the Gospel of Luke, someone asks Jesus to settle an inheritance dispute with his brother. Jesus declines, and says, in the King James Bible: "Take heed, and beware of covetousness: for a man's life consisteth not in the abundance of the things which he possesseth." The Greek word behind covetousness is pleonexia, the grasping for more. Notice he doesn't say money is meaningless. He says life doesn't consist in it. That's close to where the data landed. Income matters, often a great deal. It's still not everything.
screen: `RIVALS DESIGN ONE TEST.` · `FOR MOST, HAPPINESS KEEPS RISING.` · `FOR THE LEAST HAPPY, IT FLATTENS.` · then, large: `LIFE CONSISTETH NOT IN ABUNDANCE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: think what money can't buy you. Sit comfortably and let the breath slow. Without judging money at all, let your mind go to the things in your life that no amount of it could purchase. Someone's trust. A sibling's old joke. Your child's handwriting. A night of real rest. The way a certain friend says your name. Let one of them come forward, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Money and happiness. For most people they rise together, steadily. For the least happy, money helps only up to a point. Today's word.
Your line: not everything. Today, when a money worry comes up, take it seriously, and then name one thing it can't touch. Day one thousand three hundred forty-eight.

howItsDone: Some people pair practical care about money with a habit of naming what it can't buy, an idea scripture voices too, as in Jesus's warning in Luke about covetousness.

fork.setup: you've published a finding, and a respected colleague has published the opposite. what do you do?
options: write a sharper paper attacking theirs.
design a new study together, with a referee.
fork.reveal: Killingsworth and Kahneman did exactly that, with Barbara Mellers. the result explained both earlier findings.

original.note: Greek, in Luke 12:15, rendered 'covetousness' in the King James Bible: the grasping for more.

trapdoor: what you thought: money can't buy happiness, or money buys everything.
what it means: for most people happiness keeps rising with income, but for the least happy it flattens past a point.
what a scholar hears: an adversarial collaboration that reconciled two earlier findings; well-being rises roughly with the logarithm of income, so gains are proportional.
